triptans.summary: Triptans are medicines for treating migraine attacks, and sumatriptan is the triptan covered on this site. The NHS says sumatriptan relieves symptoms of migraine but does not prevent migraines from starting. The NHS describes sumatriptan as available as tablets, a nasal spray and an injection. The NHS says most adults can take sumatriptan, that it is not officially approved for children, and that a specialist doctor may sometimes prescribe it for a child.
triptans.mechanism: The NHS says migraines may be linked to temporarily widened blood vessels in the brain, and that sumatriptan narrows these blood vessels. Sumatriptan is a triptan, a type of medicine that acts on serotonin (5-HT) receptors. It is taken once a headache has started, not to prevent attacks. Taking sumatriptan with some antidepressants or St John's wort can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, a severe side effect.
classEffects: Feeling or being sick and dizziness are among the common side effects the NHS lists.
Flushing and tiredness are also listed.
Reactions where the injection is given or with the nasal spray can occur.
Most people have no side effects or only minor ones, and serious reactions are rare.
cautions: Heart problems, a past stroke or transient ischaemic attack, circulation problems in the legs and liver disease are listed by the NHS as reasons sumatriptan may not be suitable.
Combining sumatriptan with some antidepressants or St John's wort can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome, according to the NHS and UK leaflets.
The NHS lists high blood pressure as a reason sumatriptan may not be suitable, although it may be possible if blood pressure is now well controlled by treatment.
The NHS says sumatriptan is not taken together with ergotamine or other triptans.
The NHS says sumatriptan can be used in pregnancy if needed, with the doctor weighing risks and benefits.
The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using machinery if dizzy or drowsy after sumatriptan.
The NHS lists a severe allergic reaction and symptoms of a heart attack as possible serious reactions that need a 999 call, and says to call NHS 111 for other serious side effects.
NHS Scotland guidance on medication overuse in headache recommends limiting how often acute treatments, including triptans, are used.

5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.summary: Anti-sickness medicines that block 5-HT3 receptors; ondansetron is the member covered on this site. Ondansetron is used to prevent nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy, radiotherapy and surgery. Great Ormond Street Hospital says it is used mainly for sickness caused by chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and also after operations.
5-ht3-receptor-antagonists.mechanism: They interfere with serotonin, a natural substance that can cause nausea and vomiting, by acting on 5-HT3 receptors. StatPearls describes ondansetron as a selective 5-HT3 receptor antagonist whose anti-sickness effect is thought to come mainly from blocking receptors outside the brain. The ondansetron StatPearls entry describes an additional central action on 5-HT3 receptors in the area postrema, a region of the brain stem. StatPearls says product labelling warns about combining these medicines with other medicines that act on serotonin, although the evidence is limited.
classEffects: Feelings of warmth or flushing, mainly in the head or over the stomach
cautions: It may be given by mouth as a tablet, melt or syrup, or as an injection into a vein, according to Great Ormond Street Hospital.
The MHRA has warned of a small increased risk of cleft lip or palate after use of ondansetron in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.
A UK leaflet says ondansetron must not be used with apomorphine.
An NHS prescribing sheet says ondansetron lengthens the QT interval in a dose-related way and is avoided in congenital long QT syndrome.
The same prescribing sheet says low blood potassium and magnesium should be corrected before ondansetron is used.

MedlinePlus lists vision changes and a fast, slow or irregular heartbeat among serious effects needing urgent medical attention; in the UK, call 999 in an emergency, or contact NHS 111 or a GP for advice.

dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.summary: Dopamine antagonist anti-sickness medicines are used to treat nausea and vomiting, and metoclopramide is the member covered on this site. The MHRA has restricted metoclopramide to short-term use because of the risk of serious neurological side effects. The NHS says metoclopramide is usually taken for a short time. MedlinePlus, a US source, also describes its use for slowed stomach emptying and for reflux symptoms.
dopamine-antagonist-antiemetics.mechanism: Metoclopramide is grouped with domperidone in NHS formularies. StatPearls describes metoclopramide as blocking dopamine-2 receptors, including in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of the brainstem.
classEffects: Drowsiness, low mood or depression, and diarrhoea are listed by the NHS as common side effects.
Uncontrollable movements such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms
cautions: The MHRA says the risk of acute neurological effects is higher in children than in adults, and that in children aged 1 to 18 it is only a second-line option.
Epilepsy and Parkinson's disease are listed by the NHS as conditions where metoclopramide may not suit someone.
The NHS asks people taking Parkinson's disease medicines, drowsiness-causing medicines or other anti-sickness medicines to speak to a doctor or pharmacist first.
The NHS says uncontrollable movements such as tics, tremors, muscle stiffness and spasms are the most common serious side effect of metoclopramide.
MedlinePlus, a US source, says tardive dyskinesia, a movement disorder, may not go away after metoclopramide is stopped. Its injection page adds that the risk rises the longer treatment lasts.
MedlinePlus also says older adults should not usually take metoclopramide for those uses.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E straight away after a seizure or fit while taking metoclopramide.
The NHS advises avoiding alcohol with metoclopramide because it will make a person feel more sleepy.
StatPearls describes neuroleptic malignant syndrome as a possible complication of metoclopramide, and the NHS says to call 999 if it is suspected.

references.title: NHS: How and when to take metoclopramide

antimotility-agents.summary: Antimotility agents are medicines that slow the bowel to treat diarrhoea, and loperamide is the member covered on this site. Product information for UK loperamide medicines says it slows the bowel and increases absorption of water and electrolytes, so stools firm up. The NHS says loperamide slows the passage of food through the gut, which lets the body absorb more water, so stools firm up and become less frequent. The NHS advises talking to a doctor if loperamide bought over the counter is needed for more than a short time.
antimotility-agents.mechanism: UK and US product information describes loperamide as an opioid (mu) receptor agonist that acts on the gut wall to reduce propulsive movement of the bowel. The slower movement gives the body more time to take water back from the bowel contents.
classEffects: Constipation, headache and feeling sick are common side effects, according to the NHS.
Dizziness, tiredness or sleepiness, which alcohol makes more likely
cautions: The NHS lists severe diarrhoea after antibiotics, a flare-up of ulcerative colitis, constipation or a swollen stomach, and blood in the stool with a high temperature as situations where loperamide is not suitable.
The NHS says loperamide is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough evidence about it.
The NHS says some medicines can affect how loperamide works, including clozapine, ritonavir, quinidine, itraconazole, gemfibrozil and desmopressin.
MedlinePlus says taking more than the recommended amount of loperamide can cause serious heart problems that may be fatal.

The NHS says taking too much loperamide can cause serious heart problems. If too much has been taken, 999 or A&E is the route for urgent help; if it was taken on purpose, NHS 111 and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) can also help.
MedlinePlus, a US source, says loperamide should not be given to a child younger than 2 years because of the risk of serious breathing and heart problems.
MedlinePlus says people with a prolonged QT interval, a slow or irregular heartbeat or low potassium should tell their doctor before using it.
The NHS says a serious allergic reaction to loperamide is possible but rare.
The NHS advises not driving, cycling or using machinery if loperamide causes dizziness, tiredness or sleepiness.

osmotic-laxatives.summary: Osmotic laxatives draw water into the bowel to soften poo; lactulose is the one covered on this site. The NHS says osmotic laxatives such as lactulose and macrogol draw water into the bowel to soften poo and make it easier to pass. The NHS says they can take a few days to work. Lactulose is described by the NHS as a laxative medicine to treat constipation.
osmotic-laxatives.mechanism: The NHS says lactulose draws water into the bowel, which makes poo softer. StatPearls says lactulose has negligible absorption into the body and reaches the large bowel unchanged. The NHS describes macrogol as an osmotic laxative that brings water into the bowel, making stools softer and easier to pass.
classEffects: Stomach ache, bloating, wind and diarrhoea are listed by the NHS for both macrogol and lactulose; feeling or being sick is listed for macrogol.
Diarrhoea is particularly common with lactulose at higher amounts, and the NHS says reducing the amount may help.
cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to lactulose and galactosaemia as reasons it may not be suitable.
Irritable bowel syndrome, diverticular disease, Crohn's disease and a bowel blockage not caused by constipation are conditions where the NHS advises checking first.
The NHS says long-term high amounts of lactulose may affect blood sugar in people with diabetes.
Diarrhoea, bloating and wind are common with lactulose, according to the NHS.

The NHS lists muscle cramps or weakness and an irregular heartbeat as serious side effects of lactulose, and says to contact a doctor or NHS 111 straight away if they follow severe diarrhoea or vomiting; a serious allergic reaction needs a 999 call.
StatPearls says lactulose, like most laxatives, can cause large changes in the body's fluid and electrolyte balance, and that diarrhoea is its most significant side effect.
The NHS says it is important to drink plenty of fluid when taking osmotic laxatives, to avoid dehydration.
The NHS says lactulose is for babies and younger children only if a doctor prescribes or recommends it, and macrogol for younger children only if prescribed.

references.title: NHS: Who can and cannot take lactulose
